“Selective breeding”  is the poor man’s version of genetic engineering, and has been a human practice for over 10,000 years. Some of it has lead to ill effects for the animals involved. And it can be argued that it has enabled the domestication of animal breeds and intensive agricultural practices that have already lead to well-described disastrous consequences. For example, the histories of the Dust Bowl, or the introduction of house cats and other domesticated xenobiota and to island nations. The crises only took a couple decades to manifest. 

Meanwhile we have already pioneered gene editing, in our own children, to correct well-characterized and discrete small-sequence code defects for otherwise deadly genetic disorders. The correction of uninherited point mutations, a genetic wound, carries the benevolence of turning bad luck around. 

That Fido, and not a cereal crop bound for dissemination to unsuspecting subsistence farmers, has his itch antigen edited out seems like a trivial risk, on the level (possibly even less risky, due to the gene’s isolation) with the selective breeding practices of yore and their associated ill effects. In just a few years we will know how these two pups fare, but I hope it goes well. I’m an agnostic in the pet world but see great potential for expanding access to companionship for those who depend on (Hu)Man’s Best Friend for their survival and livelihood. Yes, the Cold War was over, and the West had won. If Jennifer wants to be truly useful, now she needs to revisit Huntington's Clash of Civilizations (1996), another collection of thoughts that was right and wrong and everything in between.

To fully appreciate what is wrong with the whole idea of an End of History, read Charles Taylor's "Interpretation and the Sciences of Man" (The Review of Metaphysics, Vol. 25, No. 1 (Sep., 1971). You can download a PDF of the essay. It's long (50 pp.) but quite readable and understandable for the intelligent layperson. There is an abridged version included in some anthologies, but it omits a lot of the best parts of Taylor's essay -- kind of like the AM radio version of "Light My Fire." Please read the long version. It's brilliant.

TLDR: There is no such thing as "human nature" and no way to objectively, "scientifically" analyze human behavior in value-neutral terms using only brute-data identifiable behavior. Every term we use to describe human action is already grounded in our own culture's concepts and infused with its values. To believe otherwise leads to disastrous self-delusions.

Who in the 19th Century could foresee the scale and speed that global trade and communication would achieve? The growing role of the Worldwide Web in influencing political opinion? The concerns about the role of artificial intelligence, or about future pandemics, natural or manmade? The effects of global warming or the rise of environmentalism?

The future will continue to confront us with surprises, and History will continue to unfold. Fasten your seat belts; it's going to be a bumpy ride.

Nadas was a giant, like his fellow Hungarian Laszlo Krasznahorkai. Greats, both, on the world stage. It's a stage that most Americans these days, I venture to think, are largely unfamiliar with--the greats of world literature the past 50 years, including those now writing. Is Marlon James among those greats?  (A Booker, or any prize really, is not, by itself a guarantee.) Time will tell. His work is ambitious and varied. (Not sure about the two volumes of the Dark Star Trilogy, however, though one could have similar qualms about Lessing's Canopus in Argos, couldn't one.) The pronouncement in the headline here is probably premature. The anointment is probably premature. But Sontag's similar pronouncement about and anointment of Nadas (which I think likely Mr. Garner would disagree with) was arguably right on the money. Perhaps this is, too.

Literary criticism often crowns a work as the "novel of the century" based on technical ambition, prose, or political scope, but that analytical framework ignores the most fundamental aspect of reading: personal alignment.
For a novel to truly hold universal weight, its core internal drives must connect with the reader’s basic human experience. When a narrative is built around attractions, psychological frameworks, or instincts that feel completely foreign to one's own natural disposition, the bridge between the reader and the text breaks. It ceases to be a meaningful reflection of life and becomes an abstract study.
Every reader engages with art through their own foundational nature. When the core theme of a book alienates you at the mind level before you even open it, no amount of critical acclaim or panel consensus can transform it into a universal masterpiece. Technical craft is meaningless if the human premise fails to resonate.

What matters is that the poem couldn’t be published in full while Pushkin was alive. For Russian culture, death can be a gateway to freedom. Just listen to the exhilaration in the 10th Symphony of Shostakovich, right after the death of Stalin. And consider the wordless quotation in the 5th Sumphony (1937) of the composer’s setting of the Pushkin poem. «Возрождение»

The U.S. Open is a magnificent but temporary event that generates approximately half a billion dollars in a very short window. The New York Knicks, on the other hand, generate substantial and consistent revenue year-round — not only for Madison Square Garden but for businesses throughout all five boroughs of New York City, regardless of wins and losses.

As a proud 37-year veteran of New York City Transit, I have had the honor of transporting thousands of fans to both events. I can tell you this: our fans love it. The conversations you hear on those trains and buses are amazing — pure excitement about the matches, about being in the heart of New York City, about being part of something bigger.

So I have a bold suggestion for fellow sports enthusiasts, team owners, management, Governor Kathy Hochul, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Let’s raise the bar for New York.

May I suggest considering Arthur Ashe Stadium as a venue for an exhibition basketball game? Additionally, once Etihad Park is complete, perhaps exhibition tennis matches could be held on real grass there.

At first I could not eat anything with lactose or galactins and was also irritated by fructans - for those of you not familiar with those terms that means no dairy, beans or wheat. Now after taking those two pills each night I can eat anything except dairy, and I’ve learned to substitute with non-dairy alternatives so my life is back to normal.

For those of you with similar issues this is what my Dr said about these drugs:

- LDN - calms immune system, kills/blocks anti-vinculan antibodies my body creating in over-reactive immune response (still trying to fight Giardia). Allows body to create vinculan which holds cell walls together tighter to block large chain protein/sugars from leaking through.
- LDE - improves cell signaling to brain to make small intestine motile to move food at night.
- And finally, as a precaution before eating anything potentially risky (which I rarely do) take Sybbzymes - helps to breakdown final sugars - take before eating

Suppose astronomers discover there is a very large asteroid, nearly at the orbit of Jupiter, headed directly for earth, and that the probability of impact was 80%, but it would be 30 years in the future. A mission to change its path would cost $10T USD, with a chance of success of 80%. So, only a 64% chance that it would hit and that we could have avoided it. Impact to the world economy wood be very significant, but recoverable in 10 to 15 years 

Let's be honest, we'd have done nothing. 

Now it's 10 years later, the asteroid is much closer, and the probability of impact is 95%, and the cost of a much larger mission to change its path is $100T USD, with a probability of success of 40%, for a overall chance of avoidance of 38%. Impact to the word economy would be devastating, likely not recoverable in 100 years or more.

It's not a perfect analogy, but you get the idea. 30 years ago was when we had a shot at stopping the worst effects of climate change. comments.body: I've been going down to Phantom Ranch for 20 years. The Box is a section of North Kaibab Trail stretching from the junction with Phantom Creek/Ribbon Falls down almost to Phantom Ranch. Here, Bright Angel Creek has carved directly into the Grand Canyon's basement rocks. The trail is cut directly into the sheer canyon walls, crossing the creek multiple times via footbridges. Water gauges in Bright Angel on a normal day average one to two feet. The problem is a storm miles away on the rim completely out of sight to hikers below can send a violent wall of water, mud, and in this case, last year's fire debris, and boulders down the creek in minutes and there are no escape routes; because, the metamorphic rock walls rise nearly vertically with no terraces or side benches to scramble up to escape a surging creek. Intense convective downpours like yesterday's rapidly erode soils on upper cliff ledges, triggering unpredictable rockfalls that funnel straight down the narrow chute. Looking up from the bottom of The Box offers only a narrow sliver of sky, meaning you cannot  monitor developing storms until rain, wind, or flooding is already underway. The standard safety protocol during monsoon season is to clear The Box before 10:00 AM, check regional radar forecasts for the North Rim before descending, and never attempt to cross bridges or trail sections submerged by raging, debris-filled water. I hope they find all those hikers that are missing.

I'm at my second home on the northern tip of Newfoundland, near the Canadian National Park Viking site. Old timers here told me that what's now the core of the house was moved here from the other side of lane in 1954. There were no roads here then, no cars, trucks or heavy equipment. Roads and electricity didn't get here until 1973. The house may have been here since the 1870s or earlier as this was part of the French Shore that disallowed settling by either the French or the English. Homes didn't have deeds until 1906, when the King made the original grants, though there were multiple families listed here on an 1880s census

A successful local fisherman bought in '56. He jacked it up from the logs it sat on, as only rock was underneath, so no cellar. The house is built of long solid wood 2x5' boards stacked vertically, so very heavy. With a lot of familial and community help placed smoothed logs underneath, and dragged it 300 feet, to where it now sits, with the addition of a kitchen L. The old-timers say that every male, nearly all current, retired, or future fishermen, in town from seven years old to ninety walked or boated over to haul on the ropes, something they knew daily in their fishery. The hauling and moving roller logs took nearly two whole days and nearly every buddy was there most of the time.

The locals also used to haul houses over the frozen harbor in the winter. They used multiple dog sleds for this and then the most primitive snow cats.

comments.name: Stephen N
comments.body: I haven't read a comic book since I was a kid, and I don't know the first thing about the Green Lantern lore.  But I don't find it at all strange that a human being drafted as a "space cop" by an alien race that doesn't understand what makes humans tick would eventually become alienated (no pun intended) and begin to show contempt for the rules set by his alien bosses.  This seems to sum up the Hal Jordan character.  The John Stewart character is harder to grasp.  His upbringing by parents determined to make him Green Lantern material is full on child abuse.  That any child raised as he was could turn out to be anything other than a psychopath or a basket case as an adult is entirely unbelievable.  Yet he is presented to us as a model marine and an archetype of the stoic, self-disciplined warrior with an artistic bent.  That the alien Guardians don't see anything wrong with his upbringing makes sense to me, since they clearly know nothing about human beings and are a species entirely without empathy.  But is the viewer really expected to take John's preternatural calm at face value?  Being raised by parents who obviously thought of The Lord of the Flies as a primer on child rearing had to have had an effect on him, and not for the better.

comments.name: MB
comments.body:
I am not as well versed in the comic books that explore the Green Lantern or Watchmen universe as many, but I am very familiar with the work of Damon Lindelof, having watched "Lost," The Leftovers" and "Watchmen." 

And I'm really familiar with Kyle Chandler - primarily via his work on "Friday Night Light," but on other shows and movies.

This stand-alone gave us John's backstory, which helped peel back some layers, but there's a lot more to go to get to what -- if anything -- makes Stewart tick.  In a similar vein, I'd like to see a similar episode that shows us Hal Jordan from 2006 to 2016 which gives hints as to why the Guardians want him replaced/succeeded with such certainty as we've seen in 2026.

Chandler can show aspects of his personality beyond the "aw shucks" and "petty" aspects that are mentioned here. He's got the gut feel needed for investigative work and, most importantly, he really cares for humans...all of 'em . Of course, he can be frustrating. But also right. And a hoot (get more back and forths with Kelly MacDonald, please). 

Back to the action next week!

comments.name: Jo
comments.body:
Isn't it ironic? No, It's Sabotage! Hal's high jinks, that is.

More than a silly shaggy dog story, it would be more satisfying if Hal was hoping to kill John's chances at replacing him. Hal generally knew John was on a mission for the Marines and was being graded by the Guardians on his performance, and got an official drunk to glean the details and destroy any chance for John to succeed. Even if the Guardians were onto Hal's shtick, he might have been hoping John would blow his stack after 9 months of suppressed emotion. If so, John would blow his chances at being the next Lantern. If not, Hal would treat it as a successful prank to rub in every now and then with the classic passive-aggressive bully's ploy of saying, "Hey, get a sense of humor. If you can't stand the heat, get out of the kitchen."  

Maybe this is overthinking it. But what are superhero stories for if not to overthink things?

Symposium comes from ancient Greek ‘symposion’, which literally means ‘a drinking together.’

From ‘syn-‘ (together), and ‘posis’ (drinking) / pinein (to drink).

In ancient Greece, a symposium was a party held after a meal where guests drank together and engaged in intellectual conversation. 

Related to Syn: symbiosis (living together), symphony (sounding together), symptom: (happening together), synergy (working together)

Related to Pinein / Posis: Potable (safe to drink), potion (a medicinal or magical drink)

Glaciers can melt stealthily, and keep a hidden hanging lake in their innards.
High altitude rubble can be glued together by permafrost, until it isn't, and that rubble can free fall into the very quiet and visible moraine lake down under, sending it off to the teaming valley.
Mountains are consequences of tectonics, they are legacy of seismic cataclysms, and a foreboding of climate change cataclysms.
Wait for the glacial rebound when Greenland or Antarctic ice shields melt.
Climate change will ultimately have seismic consequences.
